caption:
Who found the Terracotta Army? Farmers digging a well.

On 29 March 1974, Yang Zhifa, his five brothers and their neighbour Wang Puzhi were sinking a well about 1.5 km east of the first emperor's tomb mound at Mount Li. They hit pottery. Archaeologists, among them Zhao Kangmin, followed — and uncovered the largest group of pottery figures ever found. Estimates from 2007 put more than 8,000 soldiers, 130 chariots and 670 horses in three pits. Most are still in the ground.

They were not the first to strike it. Excavations near the mound found graves from the 18th and 19th centuries where diggers had hit terracotta fragments, decided they were worthless, and shovelled them back in with the soil.

The figures were assembled from separately moulded heads, arms, legs and torsos. At least ten face moulds were used, with clay added afterwards to individualise each face. Workshops were required to inscribe their names on what they made — and the sculptors signed their own names in the figures' armpits.

They were also painted: cinnabar red, malachite green, azurite blue, Han purple, faces in pink. In Xi'an's dry air the lacquer beneath the paint can curl in fifteen seconds and flake off in four minutes, which is why the warriors we see are grey.

Still open: the tomb itself has never been opened, apparently over fears for what is inside. High mercury readings in the mound's soil lend weight to Sima Qian's account of 100 rivers of mercury. And the purpose of the eleven "acrobat" figures from Pit K9901 remains unclear.

Images: a group of soldiers in the largest pit by Robin Chen; a mid-rank officer by David Castor; an acrobat torso and a kneeling figure by Gary Todd; the Reagans in the pit, 29 April 1984, from the US National Archives.
